problem: Robots navigate with raw geometric sensor data and cannot use the symbolic spatial information in human navigation cues (signs, labels, directions, maps) to reach goals in unseen spaces. Prior symbolic systems need human-built maps, work only in already-seen spaces, or use very limited symbol sets.
motivation: Human wayfinding in built environments relies on purposefully placed navigation cues, and robots need this ability to be useful co-inhabitants of such spaces. The paper observes that symbols are ambiguous and malleable, so a spatial model imagined from them must be soft and revisable when real observations contradict it.
key_idea: Represent toponyms as point-masses and spatial prepositions as springs, and let a damped spring-mass simulation settle into an imagined, malleable map of unseen space that is continually reconciled with the robot's observed locations.
insight: Trusting observations over imagination (fixed point-masses with high-stiffness springs, learned scale factors, and an exploration expansion factor) lets a robot exploit ambiguous symbols and reach human-level path efficiency. The paper reports no ablations, but the human study suggests humans seek out cues more, whereas the robot heads for its imagined goal and only updates it opportunistically. The paper also proposes negative information and long-range cue detection as future improvements.
method: Robotics-oriented grammar: relational clauses (preposition, figure, referents, context) and locational clauses (toponym, frame, x, y, distance, direction) hand-crafted to encode the symbolic information in navigation cues; perception of cues is out of scope.

Clause-to-spring translation: toponyms become unit point-masses; prepositions map to distance, absolute-angle or relative-angle springs with stiffness levels; spatial hierarchy edges become very low-stiffness distance springs.

Imagination by dynamics: new point-masses are initialised greedily, ordered by total stiffness. The system (springs + viscous friction 0.1 + expansion force away from the centre of explored mass) is integrated with Runge-Kutta until acceleration and velocity fall below 0.1.
Reconciliation with observation: observed cues add fixed point-masses connected by high-stiffness (2.5) springs, overriding imagined layout.
Scale learning: per hierarchy-level-pair scaling factors are stiffness-weighted means of observed/estimated spring lengths, replacing defaults once distances are observed.
Exploration factor: distance-spring natural lengths are multiplied by a 25% step each time the goal is not found at its imagined location, until a new cue is seen (then reset to 1).
Navigation: imagined goal location is sent as a pose goal to the standard ROS navigation stack (SLAM + planner) on an Adept GuiaBot with a panoramic camera detecting AprilTag-encoded cues.

setting.backbone: Hand-designed spring-mass dynamics abstract map + ROS navigation stack (SLAM, planner); no learned model
setting.observation: panoramic RGB camera (Occam 360°) reading AprilTags, plus SLAM/odometry; cues are decoded from tags
setting.action_space: pose goals sent to the ROS navigation stack, which issues continuous velocity commands
setting.privileged: Zoo spatial-hierarchy graph given in advance (converted to relational clauses); cue content is decoded from AprilTags, so no visual perception of cues is needed

numbers.bench: other:Zoo symbolic navigation (real-world, 5 goals x 5 trials)
numbers.eval_set_note: 25 robot trials (5 per goal) vs 25 human participants, in a fictional zoo on a university building floor
numbers.backbone: Abstract map + ROS navigation stack on Adept GuiaBot
numbers.extra: Given the zoo hierarchy graph; cues encoded as AprilTags; metric is average distance travelled (m), not SR
numbers.evidence: Table 1 Overall: Human 46.4 m, Robot 39.9 m, Improvement 11.5%

numbers_note: Only average distance travelled was reported. Per-goal robot means (m): Kingfisher 36.9, Toilets 37.6, Lion 45.6, Polar bear 40.5, Anaconda 38.9. No SR or SPL. There is no standard benchmark.
results: In a real-world zoo study, the abstract map robot travelled 39.9 m on average vs 46.4 m for human participants (11.5% more efficient, 5.3% with the two human outliers removed). It was better on 3 of 5 goals and slightly worse on Kingfisher (-7.3%) and Anaconda (-0.6%).
limitations: Cue perception is bypassed (AprilTags), and the grammar and preposition-to-spring mappings are hand-crafted.
Evaluation is a single small indoor environment with 5 trials per goal and no standard benchmark or ablations; the comparison is by distance only.
No negative information or long-range cue detection; the robot mostly chases the imagined goal instead of seeking cues. The draft has an unfinished Discussion and appendix.
builds_on: Talbot et al. 2016 abstract map with linguistic cues
